newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia pro-poll markets jittery, but rises seen.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia pro-poll markets jittery, but rises seen.

text.p: Indonesian financial markets were jittery on Wednesday on the eve of the country's general elections, but dealers and brokers said they anticipated a strong showing once the polls were over.
Volumes were low on the stock and foreign exchange markets in the morning with dealers nervous about the prospect of violence during voting on Thursday and when counting starts later that day.
Stock trading picked up later in the day, brokers said. The Jakarta composite stock index closed up 0.55 percent at 672.50 points.

The rupiah fell to a low of 2,445.25 against the dollar from a 2,442/44 open in the morning on high liquidity and on news that the Japanese embassy in Jakarta had been evacuated because of a bomb threat, dealers said.
But it recovered to 2,442.50/3.50 by the close in Jakarta. Confidence returned after police reported no explosives had been found.

The four-week election campaign, which ended on Friday, was marked by some of the worst political violence in Indonesia over the last three decades amid growing dissent against the rule of President Suharto.

But analysts have said there has been little effect on the economy although the government will need to address the issue of growing income disparities, which has been cited as the main cause for a general sense of frustration in urban poor leading to frequent outbreaks of violence.

"The general feeling in the (foreign exchange) market is once the election is over, the dollar should come off," said the treasury head of a major local bank. "People who are long on the dollar will try to adjust their positions."
But he forecast a strong dollar in the interim as tensions would persist until the election process was completed.
"Over the next three days, any trader would like to hold a long dollar position. He wouldn't like to be on the short side," he said.
Equities analysts also said the stock market should rise after the elections.
"I'm feeling more sanguine," said Tom Ingles, the head of research at ING Barings in Jakarta. "As you see politics returning to the background you'll see a re-emergence of domestic investors.
"Already we are seeing over the last couple of days institutions coming back into the market buying index-related stocks."
Other analysts said renewed confidence next week could take the index to about 680 points.
